Raze

RAYZ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To raze to completely destroy or demolish.

Fire crews could only watch as the wildfire razed three mountainside cabins in under an hour.

Worked Example

Rather than restore the fire-damaged theater, the city council voted to raze it entirely and build a public park in its place.

Tearing a structure down completely, leaving nothing standing, is exactly what raze describes.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — ras- (radere)

root — ras- (radere): to scrape, shave (Latin, via Old French raser)

Put it together

Put it together: Raze comes from Old French raser, 'to scrape or shave close,' from Latin radere, 'to scrape.' To raze a building is to scrape it away entirely, down to bare ground, leaving nothing standing.

Use the root in a new word: erase

Use the root in a new word: erase: He tried to erase the chalkboard completely before the next class arrived.

Root Check

Word Choice

Raze applies almost exclusively to buildings and structures -- you raze a building to the ground, but you wouldn't usually raze a plan or an argument.
